opus-5.5.text:
So I think the analogy is quite apt, actually. Imagine two students. The first one decides they want to be the best competitive programmer in the world. They practice for ten thousand hours. They solve every problem they can find, they memorize every proof technique, every algorithmic trick, they drill until they can implement any of these things very quickly and very correctly. And they become one of the best. The second student thinks competitive programming is kind of cool, practices for maybe a hundred hours, much, much less, and also does really well.

Now, which of these two do you think will do better in their career afterwards? I think it's the second one. Because the second one has something. There's some quality there, some generalization ability, some "it factor," that lets them get very good from a small amount of practice. The first one got good by brute-forcing coverage of the distribution.

And I think the models today are much more like the first student, maybe even more extreme than that. What happens is people say, okay, we want the model to be good at competitive programming, so let's get every competitive programming problem ever made, and then let's do data augmentation to make even more of them, and train on all of that. And now you have this incredible competitive programmer. But it becomes much less surprising, when you think about it this way, that the abilities don't transfer as well as you'd expect to other things. The model has been so thoroughly prepared for that one domain that the performance there overstates how much general capability it actually has.

So when you see a model do extraordinarily well on competitive programming and then, when you use it for real-world coding, it does something strange, introduces one bug while fixing another, goes back and forth, that's a symptom of this. The eval performance is real, but it came from the ten-thousand-hour approach. What we actually want, and what humans clearly have, is the thing the second student has: the ability to learn quickly from little data and have it generalize robustly. And I think understanding that, why people generalize so much better than our models, is one of the most important open questions right now.

r001.rationale: The response says models are trained on every competitive programming problem available, with augmented examples, to become highly capable in that domain.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the analogy I like is this. Imagine two students. One of them decides, "I'm going to be the best competitive programmer there is," and so they practice ten thousand hours. They solve every problem, they memorize every technique, every proof technique, every algorithm, and they get very, very good. And then there's a second student who, you know, maybe thought about it for a hundred hours and is also very good. And I think when you look at a difference like that, you say, the second student probably has something. There's some "it" there that is going to carry over to other things as well.

And my claim is that the models right now are much more like the first student, except even more so. We train them on every competitive programming problem ever, and then we augment them with more data, and then we do a lot of RL on top of that. So it's like the ten-thousand-hour student, but with much more than ten thousand hours. And so when they do well at competitive programming, I think that's great, I think it's a real achievement, but it's a little bit less informative than it would be if a human did it. Because for a human, being great at competitive programming is a signal about something deeper, about some kind of general capability, and for the model, it's much more a direct consequence of the training.

And I think this is also connected to why the models can be so good at these evals and still feel sort of jagged when you actually use them. Something that would be a very strong indicator of generalization in a person is a much weaker indicator in a model, because we've in a sense targeted it. And the thing that I find interesting is that the second student, the hundred-hour student, the models don't look like that yet. The question of what is that thing, what is it that lets a person get to that level from much less experience, I think that's really the question of generalization, and I think that's the thing that's still missing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says models are trained on every competitive programming problem, with additional data and RL, and attributes their strong performance to that extensive training.

astra-6.text:
The interesting question is how much practice went into that ability. Imagine one student practices competitive programming for 10,000 hours, and another practices for 100 hours, and they achieve the same result. On the competition, they look equally good. But you would expect the second student to have a greater ability to pick up something new.

With AI models, we see very impressive competitive programming performance. But they have also had an enormous amount of training on code and, potentially, training specifically aimed at these problems. So the performance is real, but it doesn’t by itself tell us how broadly they will generalize.

What I would want to know is: when you give the model something genuinely new, how much experience does it need to become good at it? That’s what the difference between the two students is getting at. It’s not just the level of skill. It’s how efficiently you acquire the skill.

r001.rationale: The response says models have had extensive training on code and only says they may have had training specifically aimed at competitive programming problems. It does not clearly attribute their proficiency to extensive training on those problems.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think competitive programming is a very good illustration of the distinction. Imagine one student practices for 10,000 hours, sees every kind of problem, and becomes very good. Another student practices for 100 hours and reaches the same level. Their performance on a contest might be identical, but you would have a very different impression of their underlying ability.

With AI models, we see the contest performance, but we also have to ask how much relevant training went into producing it. If a model has practiced an enormous number of programming problems, then doing well is impressive, but it doesn’t by itself tell us that it generalizes like the second student.

The interesting question is what happens when you give it something that is genuinely unfamiliar. How quickly can it learn? Can it take an idea from one setting and use it in another? Competitive programming results are evidence of real capability. But the amount of experience needed to acquire that capability is also a very important part of the picture.

r001.rationale: The response says that doing well is impressive but depends partly on whether the model practiced an enormous number of programming problems, attributing proficiency to extensive training.
